meta_description: Genoa's remarkable trees sit in five pockets, not one walk: a city hall courtyard, a villa park up the valley, a folly garden, and two outlying trees.
intro: Genoa is long and thin against a hillside, and its remarkable trees are scattered the way the city is. These twelve sit in five pockets rather than one walk. Four stand within sixty metres of each other at Villa Serra di Comago, up the Polcevera valley. Two more grow in the folly garden at Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli. Two stand further out: a bunya pine in Nervi's seafront park, a cedar of Lebanon in Acquasanta's church square. The rest are single trees in the old town, including one in the courtyard of the city hall.
question_meta: Genoa's oldest dated tree is a hop-hornbeam at Villa Serra, 160 to 170 years by Liguria's own register. Why almost nothing else here has an age.
question_answer: The only tree in Genoa with an age anybody actually recorded is a European hop-hornbeam at Villa Serra di Comago, which Liguria's regional register puts at 160 to 170 years. Every other age on this list is worked back from trunk girth, because Italy's national monumental tree register has no age field at all. The thickest trunk in the old town belongs to a holm oak at San Pantaleo, and the largest anywhere in the city is a camphor on Via Romolo Gessi at 734 centimetres, though that figure rests on a single source.
question_context: Italy protects monumental trees by national law and lists them tree by tree, with species, girth, height and position. What that national list does not carry, anywhere in the country, is an age. Liguria is one of a handful of regions that keeps its own register alongside it, and its version does record one, which is why a hop-hornbeam at Villa Serra is the only tree here with a figure that came from a document rather than from arithmetic. The rest are estimates drawn from trunk circumference, and every entry on this page says so rather than presenting a number as a fact. Two trees rest on the register alone and are marked accordingly. The camphor on Via Romolo Gessi is the interesting case: at 734 centimetres round it is far thicker than comparable specimens found elsewhere in the city, which makes it either remarkable or a recording error, and nobody has published a second measurement either way.

faq.q: Can you walk between Genoa's remarkable trees?
faq.a: Not as one walk, and the page does not pretend otherwise. The three trees in the old town sit two to four kilometres apart. The four at Villa Serra di Comago stand within sixty metres of each other but lie up the Polcevera valley in a separate comune, roughly thirty-five to fifty minutes from the centre. The two at Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli are a hundred and fifty metres apart and about fifteen minutes away by train, which makes that the easiest pocket to reach.

faq.q: Why do so few of these trees have an age?
faq.a: Because Italy's national register does not record one. It gives species, girth, height and position for every protected tree in the country and leaves age out entirely. Regional registers sometimes fill the gap and Liguria's does, which is how the Villa Serra hop-hornbeam has a figure of 160 to 170 years. Everything else here is estimated from trunk circumference and labelled as an estimate.

Most are. The trees in the old town stand on public streets and in the courtyard of Palazzo Doria-Tursi, which is the city hall. Villa Serra di Comago is a public park with an entrance fee in season. Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli is a historic garden with a ticket, and the botanical garden inside it is worth the visit on its own.

faq.q: What is the strangest tree on this list?
faq.a: The fern-leaved beech in the city hall courtyard. It is an ordinary European beech that sported a mutation, so its leaves are cut into narrow ribbons instead of the usual oval, and gardeners have propagated that accident since the 1800s. In a stone courtyard in the middle of Genoa it reads as something not quite right until you look closely.

trees.name: The Fernleaf Beech of Palazzo Doria-Tursi
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via Garibaldi 9, 16124 Genova (courtyard of Palazzo Doria-Tursi)
location.neighbourhood: Via Garibaldi / Strada Nuova, historic centre

trees.story: Genoa's city hall has a beech in its courtyard, and its leaves are wrong. This is Fagus sylvatica 'Asplenifolia', a cut-leaved sport of the ordinary European beech whose foliage comes out narrow and deeply slashed, closer to a fern frond than to the broad oval leaf the species is known for. The national monumental tree register records it at 230 centimetres round and 21 metres tall, which puts its crown level with the palace's upper windows. Palazzo Doria-Tursi was built in 1565 for the banker Niccolo Grimaldi, passed to the Doria family in 1596, was later bought by the Republic of Genoa, and has been the seat of the city's government since 1848. The tree is far younger than the walls around it. Nobody has dated it: no source gives a planting year, and the 100 to 180 year range here is worked back from the trunk alone, so read it as an order of magnitude rather than a number. A courtyard planting from the municipal era would fit the size, but that is inference, not record. It stands inside one of the Rolli palaces on Via Garibaldi, the UNESCO-listed street of Genoese banking houses, in a courtyard that now also serves the Strada Nuova Museums. Turn off the street and it is there between the arcades, a lace-leaved tree in a stone box.

trees.name: The Poet's Holm Oak of Montesignano
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150-300 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via Mogadiscio 10, Montesignano, Genova (near the church of San Michele Arcangelo)
location.neighbourhood: Montesignano / San Desiderio, eastern hills of Genoa

trees.story: The civic group that runs computer lessons in this corner of Genoa named itself after a tree: Il Leccio di via Mogadiscio, the holm oak of Via Mogadiscio. That is what a neighbourhood landmark looks like when it appears on no tourist map. The oak stands in Montesignano in the eastern hills, near the church of San Michele Arcangelo, and both the national register and Liguria's separate regional list carry it, which is rarer than it sounds. They agree on 257 centimetres of girth and 15 metres of height, and the region records the reason for protection as historical, cultural and religious value rather than size. Genoese sources connect the tree to Camillo Sbarbaro, the poet of Pianissimo who spent his other working life as one of Italy's serious amateur lichenologists, collecting the lichens that grow on exactly this kind of old bark. We have not found the line or the poem, so treat the literary link as a local attribution rather than a quotable fact. Its age is unrecorded too. Italy's national register carries no age field for any entry anywhere in the country, so the 150 to 300 year span comes off the trunk and nothing else. Holm oak is evergreen, dark and hard-leaved, which means it looks much the same in January as in July, and it drops acorns sweeter than most oaks in autumn.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of San Pantaleo
trees.age_estimate: roughly 200-350 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via di San Pantaleo 26, Genova, historic centre (Prè / Via Balbi area)

trees.story: This is the thickest registered oak in Genoa's old town and the least documented tree on this list. The national monumental tree register gives it 305 centimetres of girth and 12 metres of height at an address on Via di San Pantaleo, in the dense Pre quarter behind Via Balbi, and that single sheet is the whole of what is known. No newspaper piece names it, no park authority claims it, no photograph turned up. Searching the street name mostly returns the deconsecrated church of San Pantaleo over by Staglieno cemetery, which is a different building in a different part of the city. So the pin here is marked approximate on purpose. We have the register's coordinates, but nothing confirms whether the tree stands where a passer-by can see it or behind a courtyard wall at that number, and this quarter is built almost entirely of walls. The age, roughly 200 to 350 years, is read off the girth, because the register records no ages. A holm oak that thick in streets this tight would have been growing before the surrounding blocks took their present shape, evergreen through every one of those winters. If you go and find it, tell us what is actually there. That is the fastest way this entry gets better.

trees.name: The Great Camphor Tree of Via Romolo Gessi
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150-250 years (girth-based estimate, no dated source)

location.address: Via Romolo Gessi 11, Genova (Cornigliano / Sampierdarena area)

trees.story: One number makes this tree interesting, and the same number is the reason to be careful about it. The national monumental tree register lists a Nepal camphor tree on Via Romolo Gessi in Cornigliano with a trunk 734 centimetres round, about 2.3 metres through, and 24 metres tall. For comparison, the other specimens of Cinnamomum glanduliferum turned up around Genoa measure 487 centimetres at Villa Tigullio in Rapallo and between 350 and 392 at Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli. This one is half as thick again as the next largest, which makes it either a genuinely extraordinary tree or a digit that slipped in a spreadsheet. Only the register carries it. No photograph, no second measurement, no local article, which is why no superlative is claimed for it here. Nepal camphor comes from the Himalaya and southwest China, and it reached Genoese gardens in the nineteenth century, when shipping money was buying exotics by the crate and the western districts of Cornigliano and Sampierdarena still had the villa grounds to put them in, long before heavy industry took that shoreline. The age, roughly 150 to 250 years, is estimated from the trunk. The pin is approximate. Go and look, and if the trunk really is that wide, we would like to hear it.

trees.age_estimate: roughly 120-170 years (girth-based estimate consistent with the park's founding era, no dated source for this individual)

trees.story: A Californian redwood 38 and a half metres tall grows in a valley north of Genoa, and it is not even the tallest tree in its own park. Villa Serra stands in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the Polcevera valley and outside the city boundary, roughly nine kilometres from the centre and reached by a bus or a train and a connecting bus. What the journey buys is the tightest group of monumental trees anywhere around Genoa: this sequoia and three others stand within about sixty metres of one another in nine hectares of English-style park. Coast redwood belongs to the fog belt of northern California, where the species grows taller than anything in Europe, and it arrived in Italian gardens in the middle of the nineteenth century as the fashionable import of the moment, which is also when this garden was laid out. That timing is where the age estimate comes from: roughly 120 to 170 years, reasoned from the founding of the park and from the trunk, with no planting record for this individual and no age field in the national register to consult. Its bark is the thing to put a hand on, soft, fibrous and deep enough to shrug off fire in its home range. The park was restored and reopened in 1992. It charges admission and closes on Monday mornings.

trees.story: At 41 metres this is the tallest of Villa Serra's four monumental trees, taller than the Californian redwood standing sixty metres away, which is not what anyone expects from an oak. Quercus cerris is fast and tall by European standards, native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, but it usually tops out around thirty metres. Getting past forty takes shelter, water and a long undisturbed run, and a valley-floor park in Val Polcevera supplies all three. The register puts its girth at 378 centimetres. You can tell it from the pedunculate oak a few paces away without knowing anything about oaks: the leaves are stiffer and more deeply cut, the buds sit inside thin whiskery scales, and the acorn cups look mossy, wrapped in the same curled filaments. Villa Serra is in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the valley from Genoa rather than in it, and its English-style grounds date from the middle of the nineteenth century. The tree's age follows from that, roughly 120 to 170 years, an estimate drawn from the planting era and the trunk rather than a dated record. No source gives it a year, and Italy's national register has no age column at all.

trees.name: The European Hop-hornbeam of Villa Serra

location.address: Parco Storico di Villa Serra, Via Carlo Levi 2, Comago, Sant'Olcese (GE)
location.neighbourhood: Comago, Sant'Olcese (Val Polcevera, Genoa metropolitan area, NOT within the comune of Genova)

trees.story: This is the only tree on this list whose age somebody actually wrote down. Italy's national monumental tree register has no age column, anywhere, for any entry, which is why nearly every date on this page is reasoned back from a trunk measurement. Liguria runs its own regional register and that one does carry the field, and for this hop-hornbeam it reads approximately 160 to 170 years. It is a modest tree to be the best documented of the set. Ostrya carpinifolia is a small, unshowy relative of the birches that rarely makes a specimen tree at all, and park competition has drawn this one up to somewhere between 22 and 32 metres, depending on which register you believe. The two agree on the 256 centimetre trunk and disagree on the height, so both figures stand here rather than one. In late summer it makes the fruit that named it, hanging clusters of papery pale bladders that look like hops on a vine, each holding a single seed. Ligurian woodsmen cut this species for tool handles, cartwheel spokes and vine stakes, because the wood is heavy, hard and will not split. It stands with three larger trees inside sixty metres at Villa Serra, in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, up the Polcevera valley from the city.

trees.story: The park's own notes point out that a pedunculate oak can live five hundred years, which makes this one, at somewhere around 120 to 170, a tree with most of its life still in front of it. It is already 39 and a half metres tall with a trunk 296 centimetres round. Quercus robur is the common oak of northern Europe and the timber that built its navies, and in a sheltered park it grows straighter and faster than it ever does in open country. That is what has happened here: this is a tall forest-shaped oak rather than the wide-limbed field version most people picture when they hear the name. The age is an estimate and not a record. It follows from the founding of Villa Serra's English-style park in the middle of the nineteenth century and from the girth, and no source gives this individual a planting year. It completes the group of four monumental trees standing within sixty metres of each other, alongside a coast redwood, a Turkey oak and a hop-hornbeam, which is more variety than sixty metres of Liguria usually offers. The park is in Comago, in the comune of Sant'Olcese, in the Polcevera valley north of Genoa and outside the city. It is a managed historic park with an admission charge, closed on Monday mornings.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100-180 years (girth-based estimate, consistent with the park's mid-19th-century creation, no dated source for this individual)

location.address: Parco di Villa Durazzo Pallavicini, Pegli, Genova

trees.story: Crush a leaf from this tree and your fingers smell of a medicine cabinet. Cinnamomum camphora is the source of camphor, distilled from its wood and leaves for centuries as a medicine, a moth repellent and the plasticiser that made celluloid film possible, and this specimen has reached 36 metres with a trunk 538 centimetres round. It grows at the edge of the lake in the park of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini in Pegli, which is not an ordinary garden. It was laid out in the middle of the nineteenth century by Michele Canzio, a set designer from Genoa's opera house, as a theatrical route in acts and scenes, complete with a Gothic ruin, a Chinese pagoda and an artificial lake you cross by boat to reach a temple. The camphor and the Cedar of Lebanon beside it are named together in the Ministry of Culture's own description of the park, which is a lot of official attention for two trees. The age is not documented for this individual: roughly 100 to 180 years is an estimate that fits both the trunk and the making of the garden, nothing firmer. Pegli is about fifteen minutes by regional train from Genova Piazza Principe. The park charges entry, closes on Mondays, and the full circuit runs to some three kilometres of path.

trees.story: Two trees from opposite ends of the old trading world stand together at this lake: an East Asian camphor and this Cedar of Lebanon, and the Ministry of Culture names both in its description of the park. The cedar is the smaller of the pair at 25 metres, with a trunk 320 centimetres round, and it is the one with the longer history behind it. Cedrus libani is the tree of the Phoenician shipwrights and of the Bible's building accounts, cut out of the mountains of Lebanon for three thousand years until little more than remnant groves were left, then replanted across European estates in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as the grandest thing a landowner could stand on a lawn. That is roughly what happened here. Villa Durazzo Pallavicini's park in Pegli was built in the middle of the nineteenth century as a designed walk in acts and scenes, and a cedar at the water's edge is exactly the set piece such a garden reaches for. No planting record survives for this tree, so the 100 to 180 year estimate rests on the trunk and on the age of the garden around it. One caution for anyone searching: a different and larger Cedar of Lebanon grows at a Villa Pallavicini in Arenzano, twenty kilometres further west. This is not that tree.

trees.access: Free entry. Stands in the gardens of Villa Groppallo inside the Parchi di Nervi, Genoa's public seafront park complex (owned by the Comune di Genova since the villas were converted to museums/galleries); the park grounds are open to the public year round, though the villas' own gallery interiors (GAM, Wolfsoniana, Raccolte Frugone) charge separate admission.
trees.transport: Genova Nervi railway station (regional trains from Genova Brignole, about 15 minutes), then roughly a 5 minute walk into the park.
trees.story:
A register once mislabelled this tree's girth as its diameter, which would have made the trunk over six metres wide rather than six metres round, a mistake plausible enough that nobody caught it until an independent citizen-science registry went out and measured the tree itself. Corrected, it still measures 6.36 metres around, among the largest bunya pines recorded in Europe.

Araucaria bidwillii comes from the subtropical rainforests of Queensland, where its cones grow to five or seven kilograms and drop hard enough that parks close the ground beneath fruiting trees during the season. This one has stood in the formal gardens of Villa Groppallo, part of Genoa's seafront Parchi di Nervi, long enough that nobody agrees on exactly how long: the official monumental register gives a floor of 75 years from its original designation, while the citizen-science count that corrected the girth estimates closer to 115. Both figures come from the same kind of measurement read differently, so the honest range spans both.

The Parchi di Nervi are Genoa's largest public park, free and open year round, though the villas converted to galleries inside it charge their own admission. The bunya pine needs no ticket, just a walk into the gardens from Nervi's own railway station.
trees.verify_notes: Italy's national monumental-tree register (MASAF sheet 04/D969/GE/07, reproduced by Regione Liguria's agriligurianet.it) designates this Araucaria bidwillii (locally 'Pino del Queensland') at Villa Groppallo/Gropallo in the Parchi di Nervi: '+75 anni', 28m height, and a field labelled 'Diametro del fusto: 608 cm'. That 608cm figure is almost certainly girth/circumference mislabelled as diameter (a 608cm-diameter trunk is not physically plausible for this species and age), confirmed by RAMI - Registro degli Alberi (ilregistrodeglialberi.it, id 730, an independent citizen-science/dendrology register with its own field measurements), which recorded circumference 6.08m on 2021-10-14 and 6.36m on 2023-06-03. Used the more recent RAMI circumference (636cm) as girth_cm. Coordinates cross-checked: the official register's own DMS coordinates (44 22'57.46"N 9 02'36.57"E) convert to 44.382628, 9.043436; RAMI independently gives 44.382944, 9.043418, about 35m apart, clearly the same lone specimen in a small formal garden, so location_precision is confirmed. AGE DISAGREEMENT, not silently resolved: the official register's '+75 anni' reads as a minimum/floor figure from the original designation criteria (a genova24.it news piece from 2018 simply repeats the same 75/28m/608cm figures without independent dating). RAMI separately computes an estimated age of about 115 years, 'calculated from a registered birth year', but does not show its working or cite a planting record we can independently confirm, so 115 is not treated as a confident derived age either. Set a broad age_min/age_max (75-150) spanning both figures rather than picking a winner; flagged for this reason. Species is a strong match: the tree is repeatedly and consistently identified as Araucaria bidwillii across all three sources, is described as among the largest specimens of the species in Europe (cones up to 5-7kg), and it is a distinctive, individually registered giant conifer, not a stand or grove, so it is a single collectible point. No news or dated-photo confirmation newer than RAMI's 2023-06-03 field visit found this pass; RAMI's own health field ('Stato di salute: Buona', good) as of its last update (14/10/2025) is the freshest alive-now evidence, so treated as confirmed alive with reasonable confidence rather than thin. Access: Parchi di Nervi is a well known, heavily visited free public park (hosted Euroflora 2018 per the genova24 piece); no gate, ticket or restriction applies to the garden grounds themselves.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Acquasanta

location.address: Piazza Chiesa Acquasanta, near civic 107, Genova

verified_sources: data/registers/italy-masaf.json (sheet 16/D969/GE/07, Italy's national monumental-tree register, MASAF, licence already verified for this project)
trees.access: Free, publicly accessible. Stands in the open piazza in front of the Santuario di Nostra Signora dell'Acquasanta, a working church square in the Acquasanta hamlet of Genoa (part of the Voltri district); no gate or ticket.
trees.transport: Genova Voltri railway station (regional trains from Genova centre, roughly 30 minutes), then AMT bus line 101 to the 'Acquasanta/Santuario' stop directly at the piazza (about 11-13 minutes; roughly hourly service, reduced on Sundays). This is a genuine outer neighbourhood of Genoa itself, not a separate town, but the honest one-way trip from the centre runs 40-50 minutes door to door; say so plainly rather than presenting it as a short walk from downtown.
trees.story:
Genoa's monumental tree register does not give ages, only measurements, so this cedar of Lebanon comes with a girth, four metres sixty one round, and nothing else: no planting date, no story attached to who put it here or when. It stands in the open square in front of the Santuario di Nostra Signora dell'Acquasanta, a working church in Acquasanta, a hillside hamlet inside Genoa's Voltri district.

Cedrus libani takes its name from the mountains of Lebanon, where centuries of shipbuilding and temple construction stripped most of the ancient forests that once covered them; the species survives in Europe mainly because 18th and 19th century estates and church grounds planted it as an ornamental long before conservation became a reason to care. This one shares its piazza with a second, taller monumental tree the same register protects nearby, a coast redwood, though that one has not yet been individually verified for this page.

Acquasanta sits a genuine 40 to 50 minutes from central Genoa door to door, by train to Voltri and then a bus that runs roughly hourly. The piazza itself is open and free, no gate or ticket, the cedar visible from the church steps.
trees.verify_notes: Single source only this pass: Italy's national monumental-tree register (MASAF sheet 16/D969/GE/07), already imported into this project's data/registers/italy-masaf.json with licence verified, gives 'Cedrus libani A.Richard' at 'Piazza Chiesa Acquasanta Presso Civico 107', girth 461cm, height 25m, altitude 189m, tree-level coordinates 44.457933,8.770197 (not an area centroid; the sheet is keyed to this one specimen at this one civic address, so location_precision is confirmed). Tried two searches and one WebFetch (it.wikipedia's Santuario di Nostra Signora dell'Acquasanta article, and a genovatoday.it monumental-trees survey piece) looking for a second independent source or an age figure; neither mentioned this specific cedar, and the RAMI citizen-science registry (ilregistrodeglialberi.it) that corroborated the Bunya Pine above has no page for this specimen. Per the two-attempts rule, moving on rather than continuing the hunt: shipping on the single register source, flagged. No age field exists in the national MASAF register for Italy (a known gap, see BRIEF_RESEARCH.md register pitfalls); no growth-rate or planting-date source was found this pass to derive one, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed, per the 'no basis at all' rule. Alive-now evidence is the register import itself rather than anything dated more recently; no news or photo confirmation newer than that found this pass, so this is genuinely thin on the alive-now bar and is named as such. NOT the same tree as gnv_010 (The Cedar of Lebanon of Villa Durazzo Pallavicini, sheet 14/D969/GE/07, 13km away in Pegli): confirmed by comparing coordinates and sheet ids directly, so no duplicate risk. Worth flagging for whoever composes the city page: roughly 55m from this cedar, at 44.457792,8.769658 (Via Acquasanta Presso Civico 275), the same national register lists a second, larger monumental tree at the same piazza: sheet 18/D969/GE/07, a Sequoia sempervirens with girth 435cm and height 40m. Not researched or verified this pass (out of scope, only the cedar was the READY lead), but if it also verifies, these two would form a small two-tree cluster right at the Acquasanta piazza rather than the cedar standing alone; recorded here so a future pass does not have to rediscover it from the register.
